new_statements.quote: La structure du mot de base dans les trois dialectes, tay daeng (tay thanh), tay yo et tay muong, est strictement monosyllabique: CV(C)/T, (C: consonne; V: voyelle; T: ton). [...] Les trois dialectes ont développé un même système tonal de base à six tons. Le nombre des tons a pu ultérieurement se réduire à cinq, suite à des confusions qui peuvent varier selon les dialectes. [...] [6.3:] En plus de la confusion de DL1 avec DL2, on note la confusion de B1 avec B2. [...] [2:] Le dialecte tay muong décrit ici est plus précisément du tay pao. Ce dialecte, à l'instar du tay yo, n'a jamais été décrit.
new_statements.translation: The structure of the basic word in the three dialects, Tay Daeng (Tay Thanh), Tay Yo and Tay Muong, is strictly monosyllabic: CV(C)/T (C consonant, V vowel, T tone). [...] The three dialects developed the same basic six-tone system. The number of tones may later have been reduced to five through mergers that vary by dialect. [...] [6.3:] Besides the merger of DL1 with DL2, B1 has merged with B2. [...] [2:] The Tay Muong dialect described here is more precisely Tay Pao. This dialect, like Tay Yo, has never been described.
new_statements.citation: Ferlus, Michel. 2008. The Tai dialects of Nghệ An, Vietnam (Tay Daeng, Tay Yo, Tay Muong). In A. Diller, J. Edmondson & Luo Yongxian (eds), The Tai-Kadai Languages, 298-315. London/New York: Routledge. [quoted from the author's updated French version, 'Les dialectes tai du Nghệ An, Vietnam', HAL halshs-01617791, 2017]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tai Pao (Thai Hang Tong; Tay Muong of Tương Dương) is a lexical-tone language whose basic words are strictly monosyllabic CV(C) plus tone (six-tone base system, five surface tones in Tay Muong: A1 13, A2 55, B 31, C1 33ˀ, C2 53, DL 11, DS1 55, DS2 11). No source says anything about word stress or accent; with monosyllabic native words the question of stress placement does not arise in the description.
new_statements.exceptions: None concerning prominence. Lao loans create doublets (bɨan 'moon' / dɨan 'month'); no polysyllabic or sesquisyllabic structure is discussed.
new_statements.domain_note: Concerns the 'mot de base' (basic lexical word) in citation form; compounds, phrases and phrase-level prominence are not discussed. Data from three named speakers of Hòa Bình commune, Tương Dương district, Nghệ An (Vietnam); the Laos-side Tai Pao is not described.
new_statements.identity_note: taih1245 is a Glottolog Bookkeeping entry for the retired ISO code thc "Thai Hang Tong". ISO 639-3 CR 2015-018 (Michaud & Pain, adopted 2016-01-15; file, p. 2-3) states: "Thai Hang Tong (THC) is an alternative name used in Vietnam for Tai Pao (TPO) (Ferlus 2008)". The language is therefore Tai Pao = taip1250 (ISO tpo), i.e. the Tay Muong / Tay Pao dialect of Hòa Bình commune, Tương Dương district, Nghệ An (Vietnam), also in Bolikhamxay/Khammouan (Laos). Michaud's 2014 Ethnologue contribution and Ferlus 2008 use "Tai Muong / Thái Hàng Tổng" as a cover term for two sub-varieties, Tai Pao (tpo) and Tai Yo (tyj, taiy1250?), which Ferlus treats as sub-dialects of one language. The only phonological description (Ferlus 2008) covers the Tương Dương Tai Pao; the Laos-side Tai Pao and the Quỳ Châu "Tai Muong" of Pacquement 2023 (tagged tyj) are not the same data. Everything found here duplicates the taip1250 world-pass record; taih1245 should be treated as an alias of taip1250, not a separate catalog entity.

new_statements.quote: Deux de ces dialectes peuvent se subdiviser en deux sous- dialectes: le tay blanc avec ses deux variantes, nord et sud, et le tay du Nghç An composé du tayyo et du tay muong (ou min/ng). [p. 212] [...] Le mot en PT était strictement monosyllabique CV(C)/T (C : consonne simple ou groupe; V : voyelle ; T : ton). [p. 214] [...] Ces confusions se sont accompagnées d'un phénomène de dédoublement des trois tons primordiaux qui passent donc à six en formant deux séries tonales : une série de trois tons associée aux anciennes initiales sourdes ; une autre série associée aux anciennes initiales sonores. [p. 215]
new_statements.translation: Two of these dialects can be subdivided into two sub-dialects: Tay Blanc with its two variants, north and south, and the Tay of Nghệ An made up of Tay Yo and Tay Muong (or Mương). [...] The word in PT [proto-Thai] was strictly monosyllabic CV(C)/T (C: simple consonant or cluster; V: vowel; T: tone). [...] These mergers were accompanied by a doubling of the three original tones, which thus become six, forming two tonal series: one series of three tones associated with the old voiceless initials; another series associated with the old voiced initials.
new_statements.citation: Ferlus, Michel. 2006. Les écritures thaï du Vietnam. Cahiers de Linguistique - Asie Orientale 35(2): 209-239.
new_statements.locator: sec. 3 'Les thaï du Vietnam : dialectes et écritures', p. 212; sec. 4 'Système phonétique du proto-thai', pp. 214-215; sec. 8 'L'écriture lai pao', pp. 226-228 (Persée scanned text; tables 1-7 are images only)

new_statements.relation_note: Same picture as the existing Ferlus 2008 statement (strictly monosyllabic CV(C)/T word, three proto tones split into six by series, silent on stress). Adds nothing on stress; confirms the identity tay du Nghệ An = tay yo + tay muong and that lai pao is the Tay Muong (Tai Pao) script, known from only 155 lexical items in three 1872-1899 manuscripts (pp. 226-227).
new_statements.rule_in_words: A study of the six Thai scripts of Vietnam, including the extinct lai pao script of the Tay Muong of Tương Dương (= Tai Pao). It treats the word as strictly monosyllabic CV(C)/T from proto-Thai onward and describes the two-series six-tone systems of the Vietnamese Thai dialects (tay muong among them); it never mentions word stress, accent or prominence. The word 'accents' on p. 219 refers to the Siamese/Lao tone marks mai ek and mai tho, not to stress.
new_statements.identity_note: taih1245 is a Glottolog Bookkeeping entry for retired ISO 639-3 thc 'Thai Hang Tong', merged into tpo Tai Pao by CR 2015-018 (effective 2016-01-15); the language is the Tay Muong / Tai Pao of Tương Dương, Nghệ An (Ferlus's 'tay muong', one of the two sub-dialects of 'tay du Nghệ An', 2006: 212). Ferlus 1993 (index 1) describes the other sub-dialect, the Tai of Quỳ Châu = Tai Yo (tyj), from Maspero's notes. Ferlus 2006 (index 0) covers the scripts of all Thai dialects of Vietnam; its Tay Muong material (lai pao script) rests on 155 words from three manuscripts of 1872-1899.

sources.note: Tone diagram (Gedney boxes) from F0 of monosyllabic words of one speaker: A column 12-3-4 split, no split in B (like Ferlus's Tay Pao of Tương Dương, 2008: 309-311), DL merged to one tone [221] = DS4, DL syllables short (0.15 s). Nothing on stress or polysyllabic prominence. Identity: speaker calls it 'Tai Muong', also called 'Tai Yo' locally; Quỳ Châu, not Tương Dương.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent (a full-text search for stress/accent/stress/intensité/tonique/proéminence: no hits). Sec. 3 'Généralités phonétiques' (HAL p. 4): basic word in Tay Daeng, Tay Yo and Tay Muong strictly monosyllabic CV(C)/T; common six-tone base system, reduced to five by mergers. Sec. 2 (p. 3): the Tay Muong described is 'plus précisément du tay pao', called Thái Hàng Tổng by the Vietnamese, never described before. Sec. 6 (pp. 16-17): Tay Muong consonants, vowels, tones (Fig. 6: A1 13, A2 55, B 31, C1 33ˀ, C2 53, DL 11, DS1 55, DS2 11; B1=B2 and DL1=DL2 merged); informants Lô Văn…

sources.note: Describes Mène (Tai Maen, ISO tmp) from one Lao refugee speaker: initials, vowels (length only for a/aa and before stops), six tones with velar conditioning (pp. 107-110). Tai Pao (/paaw A4/) is mentioned only as a 'closely related' dialect whose forms the speaker sometimes supplied (pp. 104-105); no Tai Pao phonology; the words 'stress'/'accent' do not occur.
